lessons.title: Demand and Supply: The Market Model

steps.heading: The most important model in economics
steps.body: Having built up consumer theory (one person choosing a bundle) and started producer theory (one firm choosing inputs), we now zoom out to the MARKET level: many buyers and many sellers interacting through price. This is the demand-and-supply model, and it is the tool you will use to analyse competitive markets — large numbers of buyers and sellers, none of whom individually affects the price (no bargaining power, no 'Amazon' setting prices unilaterally).

steps.heading: The demand function and its inverse
steps.body:
A demand function Q(p) takes a price and returns the quantity demanded at that price — it is usually decreasing (higher price, lower quantity) and drawn with price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal (output convention, even though price is the input to the function).

Sometimes we work with the INVERSE demand function p(Q) instead — given a quantity, what price would make consumers demand exactly that much? Economically, p(Q) has a specific meaning: it is the maximum willingness to pay of the consumer buying the marginal (last) unit at that quantity. This inverse-demand-as-willingness-to-pay idea becomes central later when measuring consumer surplus.

steps.q: What does the inverse demand function p(Q) represent economically?
options: The minimum price a firm is willing to accept
The maximum willingness to pay of the marginal consumer at quantity Q
The average price paid across all units sold
The price that maximises total revenue
steps.explain: p(Q) tells you, for a given quantity Q already being sold, what price the LAST (marginal) unit could be sold at — equivalently, the maximum willingness to pay of the consumer who values the good least among current buyers.

steps.heading: From individual demand to market demand
steps.body:
Market demand is built up from individual consumers. If consumer i has demand qx,i(px, py, mi), market demand is just the sum across everyone:

Qx(px, py, m1,...,mN) = Sum of qx,i(px, py, mi)

Graphically, this means summing individual demand curves HORIZONTALLY (add up quantities at each price), not vertically. Market demand depends on: the price of the good itself (this is the endogenous relationship we're modelling), the prices of other goods, and the incomes of all N buyers — all exogenous, taken as given.

steps.heading: Worked example: Cobb-Douglas market demand
steps.body:
Take N consumers with identical income m, each with Cobb-Douglas utility ui = x^a y^(1-a) over cereal (x) and orange juice (y). From the consumer theory lessons, you already know individual demand: x* = am/Px.

Market demand is just N times this: Qx = N x* = N a m / Px.

Notice what market demand depends on: total income across consumers (N times m), the preference weight a, and price Px. A 'shift' in demand means a change in anything OTHER than Px that moves the whole curve — here, that's N (population), m (income), or a (tastes) changing.

steps.q: Market demand is Qx = N a m / Px. If a rises (consumers now prefer good x more), while N, m, Px stay fixed, what happens to the demand curve?
options: A movement along the curve, since Px is unchanged
The curve shifts outward — demand rises at every price level
The curve shifts inward
Nothing changes since a is not a price
steps.explain: a is a preference parameter, not the good's own price — a rise in a (holding Px fixed) means MORE is demanded at every possible price, which is exactly what a rightward/outward SHIFT of the demand curve means, as opposed to a movement along it.

steps.heading: Aggregating demand curves with a kink
steps.body: When you sum two individual demand curves that hit zero at different prices, the market demand curve gets a KINK at the price where the first consumer drops out. Below that price, both consumers contribute to market demand (steeper aggregate response); above it, only the remaining consumer's demand curve matters. This is a common source of exam questions — always check whether you're above or below every individual consumer's choke price before summing.

steps.heading: Supply: the mirror image
steps.body: Supply works the same way from the production side. A typical (inverse) supply function p(Q) is usually increasing — firms need a higher price to be willing to supply more, reflecting rising marginal costs (covered properly in the Cost Minimisation and Profit Maximisation lessons). Industry supply is the horizontal sum of individual firm supply curves, exactly analogous to market demand: Qs(p,r,w) = Sum of qi(p,r,w), where industry supply depends on the price of the good and the prices of inputs (capital, labour) common to all suppliers.

steps.q: An industry has 40 identical firms, each with supply qsi = 5p. What is industry supply Qs, and how does its slope compare to a single firm’s supply curve?
options: Qs = 5p, same slope as a single firm
Qs = 200p, flatter (more price-responsive) than a single firm’s curve
Qs = 45p, steeper than a single firm’s curve
Qs = 200p, steeper than a single firm’s curve
steps.explain: Qs = 40 x 5p = 200p (horizontal sum across identical firms). The slope dp/dQs = 1/200 is much flatter than a single firm's dp/dqsi = 1/5 — with many firms in the industry, a given change in industry quantity requires a much smaller price change, i.e. industry supply is more elastic than any individual firm's.

steps.heading: Movement along vs. shift — the rule that trips people up
steps.body: The single most common source of lost marks on supply-and-demand questions: confusing a movement ALONG a curve with a SHIFT of the curve. The rule is simple and absolute: a change in the good's OWN price causes a movement along the curve (you stay on the same Q(p) function, just at a different point). A change in ANYTHING else the function depends on — income, other prices, number of buyers/sellers, input costs, tastes — shifts the whole curve to a new position. Always ask first: 'is this a change in the good's own price, or in something else?' before drawing an arrow on your diagram.

steps.q: The price of a complement good rises. What happens to the demand curve for the good we are analysing?
options: Movement along the demand curve
The demand curve shifts inward (leftward) — less is demanded at every price of our good
The demand curve shifts outward (rightward)
No effect, since only OUR good’s price matters
steps.explain: The price of a complement is one of the 'other goods' prices that market demand depends on — it is NOT our good's own price, so this is a SHIFT, not a movement along the curve. Since it's a complement, a price rise there makes the complement pair less attractive overall, shifting demand for our good inward (left).

steps.heading: Why the slope of demand isn’t enough
steps.body: You might think the slope dQ/dp of the demand curve already tells you how responsive quantity is to price. The problem: the SIZE of dQ/dp depends entirely on the units you're measuring in (litres vs gallons, pounds vs pence) — comparing a £1 change in the price of apples to a £1 change in the price of cars using raw slopes tells you almost nothing useful, since a car costs vastly more than an apple to begin with. Elasticity fixes this by normalising: it measures PERCENTAGE change in quantity per PERCENTAGE change in price, which is unit-free and genuinely comparable across goods.

steps.heading: The formula, three ways
steps.body:
Price elasticity of demand:

eD = (dQ/dp) x (p/Q)

This is algebraically identical to the percentage-change ratio (%change in Q / %change in p) in the limit as the price change shrinks to zero — it's the same idea as any other calculus-based marginal concept you've met (MRS, MRTS): a ratio of small changes, evaluated exactly at a point using derivatives rather than approximated with large discrete changes.

Since demand curves usually slope down, eD is usually negative. Some textbooks (and some exam questions) instead quote |eD|, the absolute value, to avoid constantly writing minus signs — always check which convention a given question is using.

steps.q: A demand curve has eD = -0.3 at the current price. If price rises by 10%, approximately what happens to quantity demanded?
options: Rises by about 3%
Falls by about 3%
Falls by about 30%
Falls by exactly 10%
steps.explain: %change in Q is approximately eD x %change in p = -0.3 x 10% = -3%. Quantity falls by about 3% — and since |eD| = 0.3 < 1, this demand is INELASTIC (quantity responds proportionally less than price).

steps.heading: Elastic, inelastic, and the three named cases
steps.body: The dividing line is |eD| = 1 (unit elastic): quantity and price move by exactly the same percentage. |eD| < 1 is INELASTIC (quantity barely responds — think: insulin, cigarettes, other necessities with few substitutes). |eD| > 1 is ELASTIC (quantity responds strongly — think: a specific brand when many close substitutes exist). Two limiting cases matter for diagrams: PERFECTLY elastic demand is a horizontal line (any price rise loses ALL customers — infinite responsiveness); PERFECTLY inelastic demand is a vertical line (quantity demanded never changes regardless of price — zero responsiveness).

steps.heading: Elasticity is a LOCAL concept, not global
steps.body: Here is a genuinely important, exam-relevant subtlety: for a straight-line (linear) demand curve, elasticity is NOT constant along the curve — it varies continuously, from perfectly elastic at the price-axis intercept down to perfectly inelastic at the quantity-axis intercept, passing through unit-elastic exactly at the midpoint. So 'demand curve A is more elastic than demand curve B' is only a well-defined comparison AT A SPECIFIC POINT (e.g. where they cross) — it does not mean A is more elastic everywhere. Contrast this with a CONSTANT-elasticity demand curve of the form Q = Ap^b, where elasticity equals b at every single point — this special functional form is what makes the log-linear trick below so useful.

steps.q: Two linear demand curves, A and B, cross at a single point. At that crossing point, curve A is flatter than curve B. What can you correctly conclude?
options: Curve A is more elastic than curve B at every point on both curves
Curve A is more elastic than curve B ONLY at that specific crossing point (elasticity is local, not a global property of the whole curve for linear demand)
Nothing can be concluded about elasticity from slope alone
Curve B must be a constant-elasticity demand curve
steps.explain: At the same point (same p, same Q), the flatter curve has the higher |elasticity|, since |e|=|slope| x (p/Q) and p/Q is identical for both curves at that shared point. But because linear demand curves have elasticity that varies along their length, this comparison does NOT extend to other points — you cannot say curve A is 'more elastic' in general, only at that one point.

steps.heading: The log-derivative shortcut
steps.body: There is a second, equivalent way to write price elasticity: eD = d(ln Q)/d(ln p). You can verify this is identical to the derivative-ratio definition using the chain rule (d(ln p)/dp = 1/p is the key step). Why bother with this version? Because many demand functions used in this course are constant-elasticity forms, Q = Ap^b — taking logs gives ln Q = ln A + b x ln p, a straight line in log-log space, where the elasticity b can simply be READ OFF as the coefficient on ln p, with zero calculus required once you recognise the functional form.

steps.heading: Income elasticity and cross-price elasticity
steps.body:
Two more elasticities use exactly the same logic, just with a different 'cause' variable:

Income elasticity: xi_m = (dQ/dm)(m/Q) — positive identifies a NORMAL good (demand rises with income), negative identifies an INFERIOR good (demand falls as you get richer).

Cross-price elasticity: eX,Y = (dQX/dpY)(pY/QX) — positive means X and Y are SUBSTITUTES (Y gets pricier, buyers switch toward X), negative means they're COMPLEMENTS (Y gets pricier, less of the pair is consumed together, so X falls too).

Real-world estimates from the notes: pork in the UK has income elasticity of about 0.19 (normal, but only weakly responsive to income); beer and wine have cross-price elasticity of about 0.365 (positive — weak substitutes); two near-identical wine brands can have cross-price elasticity as high as 5.76 (very close substitutes).

steps.q: A good has income elasticity of -0.5 and a cross-price elasticity with good Y of -1.2. What does this tell you?
options: The good is normal, and X and Y are substitutes
The good is inferior, and X and Y are complements
The good is inferior, and X and Y are substitutes
The good is normal, and X and Y are complements
steps.explain: Income elasticity of -0.5 (negative) identifies an INFERIOR good (demand falls as income rises). Cross-price elasticity of -1.2 (negative) identifies COMPLEMENTS (a price rise in Y reduces demand for X, since they are consumed together).

steps.heading: Why market-level and firm-level elasticity differ
steps.body: A subtlety worth internalising: the elasticity of demand for a whole PRODUCT CATEGORY (e.g. 'cars') is usually much lower in magnitude than the elasticity of demand for one SPECIFIC BRAND within that category (e.g. a particular model). The reason: close substitutes exist WITHIN a market (rival brands, essentially interchangeable) but not necessarily ACROSS markets (there's no close substitute for 'a car' in general if you need to drive somewhere). This is why a single firm can face wildly elastic demand for its own product even in a market where overall category demand is fairly inelastic — it explains why an individual seller usually has far less pricing power than the market-level statistics might suggest.

lessons.title: Government Intervention, Welfare and Deadweight Loss

steps.heading: What does it mean for a market to be efficient?
steps.body:
In the Supply & Demand lesson we found that a competitive market settles at the price P* where QD = QS. But is that outcome actually good for society, or just an accident of where the two curves happen to cross? Welfare analysis answers this question by measuring the total gains that consumers and producers get from trading in the market, and asking whether any other outcome - achieved, say, by a government policy - could make total gains bigger.

When a government intervenes in a market - with a tax, a subsidy, a price ceiling, a quota - it inevitably changes who gets how much of the gains from trade, and very often it also destroys some of those gains outright. This lesson builds the tools to measure both effects precisely: consumer surplus and producer surplus (which measure the gains going to each side of the market), and deadweight loss (which measures gains destroyed rather than redistributed). We then apply these tools to the single most common form of government intervention: a per-unit tax.

steps.heading: Consumer surplus: the buyer's side of the gains
steps.body:
The demand curve tells us quantity demanded at each price. Read in reverse, the same curve tells us the maximum price a buyer would pay for one more unit, given how many units they already have - this is called the marginal willingness to pay, or MWTP. As more units are consumed, MWTP falls (this is exactly why demand curves slope down).

The total willingness to pay (TWTP) for qA units is the sum of the MWTP for every unit up to qA - graphically, the area under the MWTP (demand) curve from 0 up to qA. If the buyer only has to pay the market price P for every one of those units, the difference between what they were willing to pay in total and what they actually paid is pure gain to them:

Consumer surplus (CS) = TWTP minus actual amount paid

Graphically, at market price P with quantity QD, CS is the area of the region between the demand curve and the horizontal line at height P, running from 0 out to QD. When price rises, CS shrinks: buyers both pay more for the units they still buy, and lose the surplus they used to get from units they no longer buy.

steps.heading: Producer surplus: the seller's side of the gains
steps.body:
An exactly parallel idea applies to sellers. The supply curve QS(P) reflects, at each quantity, the minimum price a seller needs to be willing to supply one more unit - this minimum price is closely tied to marginal cost, defined precisely in the Cost Minimisation and Profit Maximisation lessons later in this block.

Producer surplus (PS) is the difference between the amount sellers actually receive (price P times quantity QS) and the minimum amount they would have needed to receive to be willing to supply that QS - graphically, the area between the horizontal line at height P and the supply curve, running from 0 out to QS.

At the competitive equilibrium (P*, Q*), CS + PS together measure the total gains from trade generated by the market - sometimes called total surplus. A key result is that total surplus is maximised exactly at the competitive equilibrium quantity Q* - any policy that pushes the traded quantity away from Q*, in either direction, reduces total surplus.

steps.q: Consumer surplus at the market equilibrium is best described as:
options: The total amount consumers spend on the good
The area between the demand curve and the price line, up to the equilibrium quantity
The total quantity demanded at the equilibrium price
The area between the supply curve and the price line
steps.explain: Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers were willing to pay for each unit (the height of the demand curve) and what they actually paid (the market price). Summed over all units bought, this is the area between the demand curve and the horizontal price line, from zero up to the quantity traded - not total spending, and not the supply-side area, which is producer surplus.

steps.heading: A unit tax drives a wedge between buyers and sellers
steps.body:
Consider a per-unit tax of t (a fixed amount charged on every unit sold, as opposed to a percentage or ad valorem tax). Once the tax is in place, the price buyers pay, pD, and the price sellers actually keep, pS, are no longer the same number: the government keeps the difference.

pD - pS = t

The market still has to clear: quantity demanded at the buyer's price must equal quantity supplied at the seller's price, so the new quantity Q** solves QD(pD) = QS(pS) simultaneously with pD - pS = t. Because buyers now face a higher effective price (pD > P*) and sellers receive a lower effective price (pS < P*), both quantity demanded and quantity supplied fall to the same new lower level Q** < Q* - fewer units are traded than before the tax.

This fall in traded quantity is the source of deadweight loss (DWL): all the mutually beneficial trades between Q** and Q* - trades where the buyer's MWTP still exceeded the seller's minimum acceptable price - simply no longer happen. That lost surplus is not transferred to the government as revenue; it vanishes, which is why it is called deadweight.

steps.heading: Worked example: revenue, deadweight loss and where they go
steps.body:
Take our familiar market QD = 100 - 2P and QS = 20 + 3P (equilibrium P* = 16, Q* = 68, from the Supply & Demand lesson), and suppose the government imposes a unit tax of t = 5.

Step 1: Buyers pay pD, sellers receive pS = pD - 5. Set QD(pD) = QS(pD - 5):
100 - 2pD = 20 + 3(pD - 5)
100 - 2pD = 5 + 3pD
95 = 5pD
pD = 19

Step 2: Find pS = pD - t = 19 - 5 = 14.

Step 3: Find the new quantity Q** by substituting into either curve:
Q** = 100 - 2(19) = 62
(check with supply: 20 + 3(14) = 62, matches)

Step 4: Government tax revenue is t × Q** = 5 × 62 = 310.

Step 5: Deadweight loss is the area of the triangle with base (Q* - Q**) = 68 - 62 = 6 and height t = 5:
DWL = (1/2) × t × (Q* - Q**) = (1/2) × 5 × 6 = 15

So of the surplus lost to buyers and sellers from the price wedge, 310 is recovered by the government as usable revenue, while 15 is destroyed completely - trades that would have made both a willing buyer and a willing seller better off, at quantities between 62 and 68, simply do not happen.

steps.q: In the diagram of a unit tax, the deadweight loss triangle sits:
options: Between the new quantity Q** and the original equilibrium quantity Q*, bounded by the demand and supply curves
Between the price axis and the tax revenue rectangle
Above the demand curve entirely
Below the supply curve entirely, regardless of quantity
steps.explain: The deadweight loss is the triangle-shaped region between the reduced post-tax quantity Q** and the original equilibrium quantity Q*, bounded above and below by the demand and supply curves. It represents surplus from all the trades between Q** and Q* that used to happen but no longer do once the tax is imposed.

steps.heading: Generalising the deadweight loss formula
steps.body:
Using the same linear demand and supply as before, QD = a - bP and QS = c + dP, it can be shown (by the same algebra you just did, kept in symbols) that a unit tax t reduces quantity traded by:

ΔQ = Q* - Q** = [bd / (b + d)] × t

and creates total deadweight loss:

DWL = (1/2) × t × ΔQ = (1/2) × [bd / (b + d)] × t^2

Two important features fall straight out of this formula. First, DWL grows with the square of t - doubling a tax rate more than doubles the deadweight loss it causes (it quadruples it, holding b and d fixed), which is why very large taxes are disproportionately distorting compared with several smaller ones. Second, DWL is exactly zero whenever b = 0 or d = 0 - that is, whenever demand or supply is perfectly inelastic (a vertical QD or QS curve). If quantity simply cannot respond to the price wedge, there is no reduction in trade to cause a deadweight loss - a fact that motivates the Ramsey rule for choosing optimal tax rates.

steps.q: A tax is imposed on a good with a perfectly inelastic supply curve (a vertical QS). What is the deadweight loss?
options: It is at its maximum possible value
It is exactly zero
It is impossible to determine without knowing demand
It equals the full tax revenue
steps.explain: Deadweight loss comes entirely from the fall in quantity traded, ΔQ = [bd/(b+d)] × t. If supply is perfectly inelastic, quantity supplied does not change at all as price changes, so d = 0, making ΔQ = 0 and therefore DWL = 0. The full tax burden falls on the inelastic side (here, sellers), but no trades are actually lost.

steps.heading: Tax incidence: who really bears the burden?
steps.body:
A government can legally require either buyers or sellers to hand over the tax (statutory incidence), but who actually ends up worse off - the economic incidence - does not depend on that legal choice at all. It depends entirely on the relative elasticities of demand and supply.

The side of the market that is more inelastic (less able to adjust quantity in response to the price change) ends up bearing more of the tax burden, because they cannot easily escape the market by buying or selling less. If demand is very inelastic relative to supply (buyers cannot easily do without the good - insulin is a classic example), the price paid by buyers pD rises by nearly the full amount of the tax, while the price received by sellers pS barely falls: buyers bear almost the whole burden. If supply is very inelastic relative to demand (as with housing, or agricultural land in a given season), sellers bear almost the whole burden instead, even if the tax is formally levied on buyers.

This logic - tax more heavily where responses are smallest, to minimise the deadweight loss created - is exactly the intuition behind the Ramsey rule for optimal taxation, which states that the optimal ad valorem tax rate on a good is proportional to (1/|εS| + 1/|εD|): higher taxes on goods where both sides of the market are inelastic.

steps.heading: Subsidies: the mirror image, and a common mistake
steps.body:
A per-unit subsidy s works exactly like a negative tax: it pays sellers an extra s per unit, so pS = pD + s. Because sellers receive more, QS expands; because buyers effectively pay less, QD expands too, so equilibrium quantity rises above Q* to some Q** > Q*. This looks like a free lunch, but exactly the same deadweight loss logic applies in reverse: quantity is pushed past the point where MWTP still exceeds the marginal cost of production, so the 'extra' units traded beyond Q* cost more to produce than buyers value them at - a deadweight loss triangle again, this time from over-production rather than under-production. The total cost of the subsidy to the government, s × Q**, always exceeds the combined gain in consumer and producer surplus, with the gap equal to this deadweight loss.

The most common mistake with both taxes and subsidies is assuming the side of the market that legally receives or pays the money is the side that is economically better or worse off. Always work out who bears the burden (or captures the benefit) using relative elasticities, not the letter of the policy - this is precisely the trap that made the UK's Help to Buy housing subsidy largely benefit housebuilders (the relatively inelastic, supply-constrained side of that market) rather than the first-time buyers it was nominally aimed at.

steps.heading: The firm's problem: turning inputs into output
steps.body:
A firm doesn't just decide 'how much to produce' in a vacuum - it must decide how to combine scarce, costly inputs (workers, machines, land, raw materials) to generate that output. Just as consumer theory modelled a household choosing a bundle of goods subject to a budget constraint, producer theory models a firm choosing a bundle of inputs subject to a technological constraint: what combinations of inputs are physically capable of producing a given amount of output?

This lesson builds the technological side of that problem. In the next two lessons (Cost Minimisation and Profit Maximisation & Supply) we add prices and turn this technological description into an economic one - working out the cheapest way to produce a target output, and then the profit-maximising amount to produce. But first we need a precise language for describing the technology itself: the production function, and its close cousin from consumer theory, the isoquant (playing the role that the indifference curve played for consumers).

Following Harkins' notation, we work with two inputs, labour (L) and capital (K), and one output (Q), so the production function is written Q = f(L, K).

steps.heading: Marginal product: the extra output from one more input
steps.body:
The marginal product of labour, MPL, is the extra output produced by employing one more unit of labour, holding capital fixed:

MPL = ΔQ/ΔL = ∂Q/∂L

(the partial derivative notation ∂Q/∂L is used because Q depends on two inputs, L and K, and MPL asks specifically what happens as L alone changes, K held fixed). The marginal product of capital, MPK = ∂Q/∂K, is defined the same way with the roles of L and K reversed.

We normally assume diminishing marginal product: as you add more and more workers to a factory of fixed size, each additional worker adds less extra output than the one before, because they have less capital and floor-space to work with. Formally, ∂MPL/∂L = ∂^2Q/∂L^2 < 0. Graphically, if you plot total output Q against L (holding K fixed), diminishing marginal product means the curve gets flatter and flatter as L increases - it may even turn down after some point, called the law of diminishing marginal returns.

A closely related concept is the average product of labour, APL = Q/L (total output per worker), which is not the same thing as MPL - a point we return to as a common source of confusion later in this lesson.

steps.q: The marginal product of labour, MPL, measures:
options: Total output divided by the number of workers
The extra output from employing one more unit of labour, holding capital fixed
The extra output from employing one more unit of both labour and capital
The wage rate paid to workers
steps.explain: MPL = ∂Q/∂L is specifically the extra output from one more unit of labour with capital held fixed - a partial, not total, derivative. Total output per worker (Q/L) is a different concept, the average product of labour (APL); and MPL says nothing directly about wages, though we connect the two once we reach profit maximisation.

steps.heading: Worked example: computing marginal product for a Cobb-Douglas function
steps.body:
A very common production function in this course is the Cobb-Douglas form, Q = A L^α K^β, where A > 0 is a productivity scale parameter and α, β > 0 describe how intensively each input is used.

Worked example: take Q = 10 L^0.5 K^0.5, and suppose the firm currently uses L = 16 and K = 25.

Step 1: Differentiate Q with respect to L, holding K fixed, to get MPL:
MPL = ∂Q/∂L = 10 × 0.5 × L^(0.5-1) × K^0.5 = 5 L^(-0.5) K^0.5

Step 2: Substitute in the current input levels L = 16, K = 25:
MPL = 5 × 16^(-0.5) × 25^0.5 = 5 × (1/4) × 5 = 6.25

Step 3: By symmetry, MPK = ∂Q/∂K = 5 L^0.5 K^(-0.5) = 5 × 4 × (1/5) = 4

So at this input combination, one extra unit of labour raises output by roughly 6.25 units, while one extra unit of capital raises output by roughly 4 units - labour is currently the more productive input at the margin. This ratio, MPL/MPK = 6.25/4 = 1.5625, will turn out to be exactly the slope of the isoquant at this point, which is where we turn next.

steps.heading: Isoquants: mapping out equal-output combinations
steps.body:
An isoquant is the set of all (L, K) input combinations that produce exactly the same level of output Q0: formally, {(L, K) : f(L, K) = Q0}. This plays exactly the role that an indifference curve played in consumer theory, except that output Q0 is directly measurable (unlike utility, which is only ordinal) - doubling all the output labels on an isoquant map genuinely means the technology produces twice as much from every input bundle, which is not true for utility numbers on an indifference map.

Isoquants slope downward: to keep output constant while using more labour, you must use less capital (assuming both inputs have positive marginal product). They are also typically drawn as convex to the origin, reflecting the idea that it becomes progressively harder to substitute one input for the other as you use more and more of it in place of the other.

The slope of the isoquant at any point is called the marginal rate of technical substitution, MRTS - the direct producer-theory analogue of the MRS from consumer theory.

steps.q: An isoquant differs from an indifference curve mainly because:
options: Isoquants slope upward while indifference curves slope downward
The output labels on an isoquant map are directly measurable and meaningful, unlike ordinal utility numbers
Isoquants use only one input while indifference curves use two goods
There is no MRTS equivalent to MRS for isoquants
steps.explain: Both isoquants and indifference curves slope downward and have an MRTS/MRS describing their slope. The key difference is that output Q is cardinally measurable - doubling every isoquant label genuinely means twice as much output from every input bundle - whereas utility numbers are only ordinal, so doubling all utility labels changes nothing about the underlying preferences.

steps.heading: Deriving MRTS from marginal products
steps.body:
We can derive a precise formula for the MRTS using the total differential technique used for the MRS in consumer theory. Take the total differential of the production function:

dQ = (∂Q/∂L) dL + (∂Q/∂K) dK = MPL × dL + MPK × dK

Along an isoquant, output is constant, so dQ = 0:

MPL × dL = -MPK × dK

Rearranging for the slope dK/dL along the isoquant (holding Q = Q0) gives:

MRTSL,K = dK/dL (along Q=Q0) = -MPL/MPK

In our worked Cobb-Douglas example above, at L=16, K=25 we found MPL = 6.25 and MPK = 4, so MRTSL,K = -6.25/4 = -1.5625: at this point, the firm could give up roughly 1.56 units of capital for one extra unit of labour and produce exactly the same output. Notice the formula mirrors MRS = -MUx/MUy from consumer theory exactly, with output replacing utility and (L,K) replacing (x,y).

steps.heading: Returns to scale: what happens if you scale up every input together?
steps.body:
A separate question from marginal product is: what happens to output if you increase all inputs by the same proportion at once - say, doubling both labour and capital together? This is returns to scale, formally defined via a homogeneous production function:

f(tL, tK) = t^m f(L, K) = t^m Q

for some constant m. If m > 1, output more than doubles when inputs double: increasing returns to scale (IRS). If m = 1, output exactly doubles: constant returns to scale (CRS). If m < 1, output less than doubles: decreasing returns to scale (DRS).

For the Cobb-Douglas function Q = A L^α K^β, there is a very clean rule: f(tL,tK) = A(tL)^α(tK)^β = t^(α+β) A L^α K^β, so m = α+β exactly. Therefore: α+β > 1 implies IRS, α+β = 1 implies CRS, and α+β < 1 implies DRS. In our worked example, Q = 10L^0.5K^0.5 has α+β = 0.5+0.5 = 1, so this technology exhibits constant returns to scale: doubling both labour and capital exactly doubles output.

steps.q: A firm's production function is Q = 4 L^0.4 K^0.4. What kind of returns to scale does it exhibit?
options: Increasing returns to scale, since 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8 < 1
Decreasing returns to scale, since 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8 < 1
Constant returns to scale, since both exponents are equal
Cannot be determined without specific input values
steps.explain: For a Cobb-Douglas function Q = A L^α K^β, returns to scale is determined by comparing α+β to 1. Here α+β = 0.4+0.4 = 0.8 < 1, so the function exhibits decreasing returns to scale: doubling both L and K less than doubles output. This holds at every input level, since Cobb-Douglas homogeneity does not depend on the specific values of L and K used.

steps.heading: Common mistake: diminishing marginal product is not the same as decreasing returns to scale
steps.body:
This is one of the most persistent points of confusion in producer theory, so it is worth stating very explicitly: a production function can have diminishing marginal product in each input separately, while still exhibiting constant (or even increasing) returns to scale overall. These are two entirely different experiments.

Diminishing marginal product asks: what happens if I add more of ONE input, holding the OTHER input fixed? Returns to scale asks: what happens if I scale up ALL inputs together, by the same proportion?

Concretely, take f(L,K) = L^α K^β with 0 < α < 1 and 0 < β < 1. Because each exponent is less than 1, MPL and MPK are each individually diminishing (∂MPL/∂L = α(α-1)L^(α-2)K^β < 0 whenever α < 1). But if additionally α+β = 1 exactly (for instance α=β=0.5, as in our worked example), the function has constant returns to scale even though each individual input shows diminishing marginal product. There is no contradiction: adding labour alone runs into a fixed amount of capital (hence diminishing MPL), while adding both together avoids that problem entirely (hence CRS). Never infer the returns-to-scale classification from a statement about diminishing marginal product, or vice versa - always check them via their two separate, different definitions.

steps.heading: Why minimise cost before maximising profit?
steps.body:
In the Production & Isoquants lesson we described a firm's technology: which combinations of labour L and capital K can produce a given output Q. But a firm doesn't only care about what is technologically possible - it cares about cost. If two input combinations both produce exactly 100 units of output, a profit-seeking firm will always choose the cheaper one, regardless of which combination it 'prefers' on any other grounds.

Harkins' approach (and the one we follow throughout this course) breaks the firm's overall profit-maximisation problem into two steps, which give exactly the same answer as solving everything at once but are usually much easier to work through:

Step 1: For a given target output Q0, find the cheapest combination of inputs that can produce it - this is cost minimisation, the subject of this lesson.

Step 2: Given that cheapest-cost way of producing any quantity, choose the quantity that maximises profit - this is the subject of the next lesson, Profit Maximisation & Supply.

This lesson focuses entirely on Step 1. We reuse the isoquant machinery from the previous lesson (particularly MRTS = -MPL/MPK) and combine it with input prices to find the actual cost-minimising input bundle.

steps.heading: Economic cost: it is not just what you write a cheque for
steps.body:
Before setting up the maths, it is worth being precise about what 'cost' means to an economist, because this differs from everyday accounting. The economic cost of using any input is its opportunity cost: what that input would have earned in its next-best alternative use. This includes explicit costs (direct monetary payments, like wages and rent) and implicit costs (foregone opportunities, like the income an owner-manager could have earned working elsewhere).

A crucial related idea is the sunk cost: a cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered or avoided by any future decision. Because a sunk cost cannot be changed by what you decide to do next, it should play no role in forward-looking economic decisions. For example, a factory that has already paid a £10,000 fine for past pollution should not let that fine affect how much to produce going forward: the fine is fixed regardless of today's production choice, so it is not an economic cost of today's production, even though it appears on this year's accounts.

This lesson builds a model of cost that is entirely forward-looking: total cost TC = wL + rK, where w is the price of labour (the wage) and r is the price of capital (the rental rate).

steps.q: A firm already spent £50,000 developing a product that turned out to be unsellable. Should this £50,000 affect the firm's decision about whether to spend more money marketing it?
options: Yes - the firm must recoup the original £50,000 before making any new decisions
No - the £50,000 is a sunk cost and cannot be changed by any future decision, so it is irrelevant to whether further spending is worthwhile
Yes, but only if the marketing budget is also £50,000
No, because sunk costs are always equal to zero
steps.explain: The £50,000 is already spent and unrecoverable regardless of what the firm does next - it is a sunk cost. The only economically relevant question going forward is whether the future marketing spend will generate future revenue exceeding that future spend; the past £50,000 changes nothing about that comparison and should be ignored.

steps.heading: Isocost lines and the tangency condition
steps.body:
An isocost line shows all combinations of L and K that cost the firm exactly the same total amount, TC: rearranging TC = wL + rK gives K = TC/r - (w/r)L, a straight line with vertical intercept TC/r and slope -w/r (exactly analogous to the budget line from consumer theory, with input prices w and r playing the role of good prices).

To produce a target output Q0 at minimum cost, the firm wants to reach the isoquant for Q0 using the lowest possible isocost line - graphically, this means sliding the isocost line inward until it is just tangent to the Q0 isoquant. At any point where the isocost line crosses the isoquant (rather than being tangent to it), the firm could reduce cost while still producing Q0 by moving along the isoquant towards the tangency point - so a crossing point can never be cost-minimising.

At the tangency point, the slope of the isoquant (MRTSL,K = -MPL/MPK) exactly equals the slope of the isocost line (-w/r):

MPL/MPK = w/r

This has a clean interpretation: the rate at which the firm can technologically trade off labour for capital (MRTS) must equal the rate at which the market allows it to trade off labour for capital in terms of cost (w/r).

steps.heading: Worked example: solving the cost minimisation problem
steps.body:
Take Q = L^α K^β, with input prices w (labour) and r (capital), and target output Q0. Set up the Lagrangian:

ℒ = wL + rK + λ(Q0 - L^α K^β)

First-order conditions:

∂ℒ/∂L = w - λαL^(α-1)K^β = 0
∂ℒ/∂K = r - λβL^α K^(β-1) = 0
∂ℒ/∂λ = Q0 - L^α K^β = 0

Dividing the first two conditions: w/r = (αK)/(βL), which rearranges to K = L(w/r)(β/α) - exactly the tangency condition from the previous step, written out explicitly.

Substituting this expression for K into the constraint L^α K^β = Q0 and solving gives the conditional (or 'derived') factor demands:

L* = Q0^(1/(α+β)) × (αr/βw)^(β/(α+β))
K* = Q0^(1/(α+β)) × (βw/αr)^(α/(α+β))

These are called conditional factor demands because they are conditional on the target output Q0 - they tell you the cheapest input bundle for that specific Q0, not the profit-maximising output level itself (that choice comes in the next lesson).

steps.q: At the cost-minimising input bundle, what condition must hold?
options: MPL = MPK exactly
MPL/MPK = w/r, i.e. the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line
L = K, so both inputs are used in equal quantities
w = r, so both input prices must be equal
steps.explain: Cost minimisation requires the slope of the isoquant (MRTS = -MPL/MPK) to equal the slope of the isocost line (-w/r), i.e. MPL/MPK = w/r. There is no general requirement that MPL=MPK, that L=K, or that the input prices themselves be equal - those would only coincidentally hold for specific parameter values.

steps.heading: From conditional demands to the cost function
steps.body:
Once we know the cheapest input bundle L*(w,r,Q) and K*(w,r,Q) for any output Q, we can substitute back into TC = wL + rK to get the firm's (long-run) total cost function, C(w,r,Q) - the minimum possible cost of producing each level of output Q, given input prices w and r.

Two derived concepts matter throughout the rest of this course:

Average cost, AC(w,r,Q) = C(w,r,Q)/Q - cost per unit of output.

Marginal cost, MC(w,r,Q) = ∂C(w,r,Q)/∂Q - the extra cost of producing one more unit of output.

These two are linked by a simple but important relationship: AC is falling in Q exactly when MC < AC (an extra unit costing less than the current average pulls the average down); AC is rising in Q exactly when MC > AC; and AC is at its minimum exactly when MC = AC. This is the same 'marginal pulls the average' logic that applies to any average - your grade average rises only when your next module's mark exceeds your current average, and falls only when it is below it.

steps.heading: Worked example: the cost function for Q = L^0.5 K^0.5
steps.body:
Continuing the running Cobb-Douglas example with α = β = 0.5 (constant returns to scale, from the Production & Isoquants lesson), substituting into the general cost function formula gives:

TC = wQ0^(1/(α+β))(αr/βw)^(β/(α+β)) + rQ0^(1/(α+β))(βw/αr)^(α/(α+β))

With α = β = 0.5, this simplifies (since 1/(α+β) = 1 and β/(α+β) = α/(α+β) = 1/2) to:

TC = wQ(r/w)^0.5 + rQ(w/r)^0.5 = 2Q(wr)^0.5

Suppose w = r = 4. Then TC = 2Q × (4×4)^0.5 = 2Q × 4 = 8Q.

Notice this cost function is linear in Q: AC = TC/Q = 8 (constant) and MC = ∂TC/∂Q = 8 (also constant). AC = MC everywhere - exactly as the 'marginal pulls the average' rule predicts when the average never changes. This flat AC/MC is a direct consequence of the underlying constant returns to scale technology: with CRS, output increases proportionally with cost, so average and marginal cost are both constant and equal to each other at every output level.

steps.q: A firm's average cost curve AC(Q) is currently falling as Q increases. What must be true of marginal cost MC at this output level?
options: MC must be greater than AC
MC must be less than AC
MC must equal AC exactly
Nothing can be said about MC without more information
steps.explain: AC falls when the next unit produced costs less than the current average - pulling the average down. This means MC < AC whenever AC is falling. Conversely, MC > AC whenever AC is rising, and MC = AC exactly at the minimum point of a U-shaped AC curve.

steps.heading: Short run versus long run: the fixed input
steps.body:
Everything so far assumed the firm is free to choose both L and K - this is the long run. In the short run, at least one input (conventionally capital, K with a bar denoting 'fixed') is stuck at some pre-committed level, and the firm can only adjust labour. Short-run total cost becomes TC = wL + r×Kfixed, splitting into total variable cost (wL, which changes as output changes) and total fixed cost (r×Kfixed, paid no matter how much - or how little - the firm produces).

Because the firm cannot freely substitute towards the technologically ideal input mix in the short run, short-run cost of producing any given Q is generally higher than long-run cost of producing that same Q. Graphically, the short-run average cost (SAC) curve touches the long-run average cost (LAC) curve at exactly one point - the output level for which the fixed capital happens to be the cost-minimising choice - and lies above it everywhere else. As the fixed capital level varies, we get a whole family of SAC curves, and the LAC curve is their lower envelope: the boundary formed by tracing out the lowest point reachable by any SAC curve at each output level.

steps.heading: Common mistake: do not confuse cost minimisation with profit maximisation
steps.body:
A very frequent error is to treat the cost-minimisation problem in this lesson as though it already tells you how much the firm should produce. It does not. Cost minimisation answers a conditional question: 'given that the firm has decided to produce Q0 units (for whatever reason), what is the cheapest way to do it?' It says nothing about whether Q0 is actually the output level that maximises the firm's profit - that requires bringing in the output price and comparing marginal revenue to marginal cost, which is exactly the subject of the next lesson.

A second closely related mistake: the conditional factor demands L*(w,r,Q) and K*(w,r,Q) derived in this lesson are not the same objects as the unconditional input demands you get once you also optimise over Q in the profit maximisation problem - although, reassuringly, once you plug the profit-maximising Q* into these conditional demand functions, you get exactly the same input choices the firm would make solving the whole problem in one step at once. We verify this equivalence explicitly at the start of the next lesson.

lessons.title: Profit Maximisation & the Firm's Supply Curve

steps.heading: From cost minimisation to profit maximisation
steps.body:
The Cost Minimisation lesson found, for any target output Q, the cheapest way to produce it: the cost function C(w,r,Q). That still leaves one question unanswered: how much should the firm actually produce? This lesson answers that question, completing Harkins' two-step approach to the firm's problem.

Assume the firm is a price taker in both the output market (it sells at a fixed market price p, unable to influence it by producing more or less) and the input markets (it buys labour and capital at fixed prices w and r). The firm's profit is:

π = Total Revenue - Total Cost = pQ - C(w,r,Q)

Step 2 of the two-step approach is to choose Q to maximise this expression, treating C(w,r,Q) as already known from Step 1. Because this is now a function of the single variable Q (with L and K already optimised out via the cost-minimisation problem), it is an unconstrained maximisation problem - no Lagrangian required, just an ordinary first-order condition.

steps.heading: The profit-maximising output rule: price equals marginal cost
steps.body:
Differentiate π = pQ - C(w,r,Q) with respect to Q and set the derivative to zero:

∂π/∂Q = p - ∂C(w,r,Q)/∂Q = 0

p = ∂C(w,r,Q)/∂Q = MC(Q)

This is one of the most important results in microeconomics: a price-taking, profit-maximising firm produces up to the point where price equals marginal cost. The intuition is straightforward: if producing one more unit brings in revenue p that exceeds the marginal cost MC of producing it, the firm gains by producing that extra unit - so it should keep expanding output as long as p > MC. If instead MC > p, the last unit produced cost more than it earned, so the firm should cut back. Only at p = MC is there no further gain available in either direction.

A subtlety worth flagging now (we return to it properly later): because the firm should keep expanding whenever p > MC, marginal cost must be increasing (sloping upward) at the profit-maximising quantity - only the upward-sloping portion of the MC curve is ever relevant to profit maximisation.

steps.q: A price-taking firm currently produces where price exceeds marginal cost (p > MC). To increase profit, it should:
options: Reduce output, since MC will fall
Increase output, since each additional unit adds more revenue than cost
Keep output unchanged, since profit is already maximised
Shut down immediately
steps.explain: As long as price exceeds marginal cost, producing one more unit brings in p in revenue while costing only MC to produce - a net gain. The firm should keep expanding output until p = MC exactly, at which point no further expansion adds to profit. This is the core logic behind the profit-maximising rule p = MC.

steps.heading: Worked example: the two-step solution for a Cobb-Douglas firm
steps.body:
Take Q = L^(1/3)K^(1/3) (so α = β = 1/3, giving α+β = 2/3 < 1 - decreasing returns to scale, following the definitions from the Production & Isoquants lesson). Using the general cost function formula from the Cost Minimisation lesson with these exponents gives (after substituting and simplifying):

TC = 2Q^(3/2)(rw)^(1/2)

Step 1: Write profit as a function of Q alone:
π = pQ - 2Q^(3/2)(rw)^(1/2)

Step 2: Differentiate with respect to Q and set to zero (apply p = MC):
p = 3Q^(1/2)(rw)^(1/2)

Step 3: Solve for the profit-maximising output, Q*:
Q* = p^2 / (9rw)

Step 4: Substitute back to find maximised profit:
π* = p^3 / (27rw)

Suppose specifically p = 9, w = r = 1. Then Q* = 81/9 = 9, and π* = 729/27 = 27. You can check this is indeed optimal: at Q slightly below 9, price (9) exceeds marginal cost 3Q^0.5, so expanding pays; at Q slightly above 9, marginal cost exceeds price, so contracting pays.

steps.heading: The one-step problem: an equivalent way to solve the same problem
steps.body:
Instead of first minimising cost and then choosing Q, we could instead choose L and K directly to maximise profit in one go:

maximise over L,K: π = pQ - wL - rK = p×f(L,K) - wL - rK

This is again unconstrained (no Lagrangian needed, since the firm is simply free to pick any L, K it likes and accept whatever output results). The first-order conditions are:

p × ∂f(L,K)/∂L - w = 0, which gives p × MPL = w
p × ∂f(L,K)/∂K - r = 0, which gives p × MPK = r

Each condition has a clean interpretation: p × MPL is the value of the marginal product of labour - the extra revenue generated by hiring one more worker. The firm hires labour up to the point where this value exactly equals the wage w; beyond that point, the extra worker costs more than the revenue they generate.

Solving these two conditions simultaneously for L*(w,r,p) and K*(w,r,p), then substituting into f(L,K) to get Q*(w,r,p), gives exactly the same supply function and exactly the same profit π* = pQ* - wL* - rK* as the two-step approach above - a fact you should convince yourself of directly using the Q=L^(1/3)K^(1/3) example above.

steps.q: At the profit-maximising input choice, the condition p × MPL = w means:
options: The wage rate determines the price of output
Labour costs exactly as much as capital
The value of the extra output produced by one more worker exactly equals the cost of hiring them
Labour productivity is zero at the optimum
steps.explain: p × MPL is the value of the marginal product of labour: the extra output from one more worker (MPL), valued in money terms at the market price p. Profit maximisation requires hiring labour up to the point where this value exactly equals the wage w - hiring further would cost more than the extra revenue generated, while stopping earlier would leave profitable hires unmade.

steps.heading: The profit function and its properties
steps.body:
Solving either version of the problem gives the firm's profit function, π(w,r,p) - the maximum profit achievable at given input and output prices. Three properties recur throughout applied microeconomics:

π(w,r,p) is increasing in p (a higher output price can only help - the firm could always keep producing exactly what it did before and earn more) and decreasing in w and r (higher input prices can only hurt, or leave profit unchanged if that input is not being used).

π(w,r,p) is homogeneous of degree 1 in (w,r,p): if all three prices double, profit exactly doubles too. Intuitively, this is just a unit-of-account change - if wages, rental rates and the output price all double simultaneously, nothing real has changed about the firm's optimal choices, so real profit in the new units is simply twice the old number.

Graphically, isoprofit lines (analogous to isoquants and isocosts) show combinations of inputs and output that yield the same level of profit; the profit-maximising point is where the production function reaches the highest attainable isoprofit line, mirroring how cost minimisation found the lowest attainable isocost line tangent to a fixed isoquant.

steps.heading: From marginal cost to the supply curve
steps.body:
The condition p = MC(Q), derived earlier, effectively already tells us the supply function: for any output price p, it gives the quantity Q* the firm wants to supply. But there is a missing piece: the firm always has the option of producing Q = 0 instead, and it will exercise that option whenever producing anything would leave it worse off than shutting down entirely.

In the long run, the firm shuts down (chooses Q = 0) whenever price falls below average cost, P < AC(Q) at every Q, because it cannot even cover the full cost of production. In the short run, since fixed costs must be paid regardless of output level, the firm keeps producing as long as price at least covers average variable cost, P ≥ AVC(Q), even if it does not fully cover average total cost - producing something at least contributes towards the unavoidable fixed cost, which would otherwise be lost entirely.

Putting this together: the firm's supply curve is the upward-sloping portion of its MC curve that lies above AC (long run) or above AVC (short run); below that threshold, the firm supplies zero. This is why short-run supply tends to be flatter (more elastic, in the language of the Elasticities lesson) than long-run supply, since in the short run at least one input is fixed and cannot adjust.

steps.q: In the long run, at what price does a price-taking firm choose to produce zero output?
options: Whenever price is below marginal cost at every output level
Whenever price is below average cost at every output level, i.e. the firm cannot cover its full costs
Whenever price falls at all, even slightly, from its previous level
Never - firms always produce a positive quantity in the long run
steps.explain: In the long run all costs, including fixed costs, must be covered for production to be worthwhile. If price P is below average cost AC(Q) for every possible Q, the firm cannot find any output level that avoids a loss, so it produces nothing at all and earns zero profit rather than a guaranteed loss. In the short run the relevant threshold is lower - average variable cost AVC - because fixed costs are sunk and must be paid regardless of the output decision.

steps.heading: Common mistake: profit function homogeneity is not the same as supply function homogeneity
steps.body:
Students frequently mix up two closely related but distinct homogeneity results. The profit function π(w,r,p) is homogeneous of degree 1 in prices: doubling w, r and p together exactly doubles profit. The supply function Q*(w,r,p), by contrast, is homogeneous of degree 0 in prices: doubling w, r and p together leaves the profit-maximising quantity completely unchanged.

The reasoning is straightforward once you see it: doubling all prices simultaneously is equivalent to just relabelling the currency - it changes nothing real about the underlying trade-off between producing more or less, since both the extra revenue and the extra cost of one more unit scale by exactly the same factor. So the profit-maximising quantity itself is unaffected (degree 0), even though the money value of profit, measured in the new currency units, does double (degree 1). You can verify this directly from Q* = p^2/(9rw) derived earlier: replacing p, w, r with 2p, 2w, 2r gives Q* = (2p)^2/(9×2r×2w) = 4p^2/(36rw) = p^2/(9rw), exactly unchanged.

A second common mistake, already flagged in the Cost Minimisation lesson but worth repeating here: never apply the profit-maximisation condition p = MC without checking that the resulting output is actually worth producing at all - i.e. that price at least covers average (variable) cost. A firm can satisfy p = MC at some Q > 0 and still be better off shutting down completely if that price is below the relevant average cost threshold.

steps.heading: Three ways to measure a welfare change
steps.body: The Government Intervention & Welfare lesson introduced Consumer Surplus (CS) as a way to measure how a price change affects a consumer, using the area under the ordinary (Marshallian) demand curve. But CS has a subtle limitation: it mixes together substitution AND income effects, evaluated at a single fixed income level — which means it isn't quite measuring 'how much money would fix this' in a fully precise way. Economists use two more precise, Hicksian-demand-based measures for exactly this purpose: Compensating Variation (CV) and Equivalent Variation (EV). Both put a pound value on a welfare change, but they ask two subtly different questions.

steps.heading: Compensating Variation
steps.body:
CV answers: how much money would the government need to give the consumer AFTER a price rise, to make them EXACTLY as well off as they were before it?

Graphically: take the NEW (post-price-change) budget line, and shift it OUTWARD (give more income) until it becomes tangent to the ORIGINAL indifference curve. The size of that shift, in money, is CV.

Formally, using the expenditure (Hicksian cost) function e(p1,p2,u), and letting u0 be the ORIGINAL (pre-change) utility level:

CV = e(p1', p2, u0) - e(p1, p2, u0)

where p1' is the new price and p1 is the old price. Both terms use the SAME reference utility u0 — that consistency is what makes CV well-defined.

steps.heading: Equivalent Variation
steps.body:
EV answers a mirror-image question: how much money would have to be TAKEN AWAY from the consumer BEFORE the price rise, to leave them just as badly off as they'd actually be AFTER it? Equivalently, EV is the maximum amount the consumer would be willing to pay to AVOID the price change happening at all.

Graphically: take the ORIGINAL (pre-price-change) budget line, and shift it INWARD (take away income) until it becomes tangent to the NEW indifference curve. The size of that shift is EV.

Formally, letting u1 be the NEW (post-change) utility level:

EV = e(p1, p2, u1) - e(p1', p2, u1)

Notice EV uses u1 throughout (the new utility), just as CV used u0 throughout (the original utility) — each measure is internally consistent, but they use DIFFERENT reference utility levels from each other, which is exactly why they can give different numbers for the same price change.

steps.q: CV and EV are both built from Hicksian expenditure functions, but at different reference utility levels. Which utility level does each use throughout its own formula?
options: CV uses the new utility u1; EV uses the original utility u0
CV uses the ORIGINAL utility u0 throughout; EV uses the NEW utility u1 throughout
Both use the average of u0 and u1
Neither uses a fixed utility level — both vary utility along the calculation
steps.explain: CV asks 'how much money restores the ORIGINAL wellbeing u0 at the new prices', so it fixes u0 throughout. EV asks 'how much money at the OLD prices would match the NEW wellbeing u1', so it fixes u1 throughout. Using a consistent reference utility in each is what keeps each measure well-defined.

steps.heading: Worked example: computing CV and EV
steps.body:
Take U(x1,x2)=x1^0.5x2^0.5, p2=1, M=100. The price of good 1 rises from p1=1 to p1=4. For Cobb-Douglas with α=0.5, the expenditure function is e(p1,p2,u)=2u·√(p1p2).

Step 1 — find the original utility u0: at p1=1, x1*=0.5(100)/1=50, x2*=50, so u0=√(50×50)=50.

Step 2 — find the new utility u1: at p1=4 (same income M=100), x1*=0.5(100)/4=12.5, x2*=50, so u1=√(12.5×50)=√625=25.

Step 3 — compute CV, using u0 throughout: CV = e(4,1,50) - e(1,1,50) = 2(50)√4 - 2(50)√1 = 200 - 100 = £100. (Notice e(1,1,50)=100 exactly matches the original income M — this is always true, since u0 is precisely the utility that M actually achieves at the original prices.)

Step 4 — compute EV, using u1 throughout: EV = e(1,1,25) - e(4,1,25) = 2(25)(1) - 2(25)(2) = 50 - 100 = -£50, i.e. a magnitude of £50 (the sign convention here reflects EV as 'income lost'; economically, the consumer would be willing to give up £50 of their ORIGINAL income to avoid the price rise happening at all).

So for this price RISE: CV=£100, EV=£50 — CV is the larger of the two, which is the typical pattern for a price rise in a normal good.

steps.q: In the worked example, why are CV (£100) and EV (£50) different numbers for the exact same £1→£4 price rise in good 1?
options: One of the two calculations must contain an arithmetic error

Because CV is evaluated using the ORIGINAL (richer-feeling) utility level u0=50, while EV is evaluated using the NEW (poorer-feeling) utility level u1=25 — since there is a genuine income effect, the marginal value of money differs between these two reference points, so the two measures need not match
Because EV always equals exactly half of CV as a general rule
Because Cobb-Douglas preferences make CS, CV and EV always disagree, unlike any other utility function
steps.explain: CV and EV both correctly answer their OWN specific question, but those questions are evaluated at different utility levels (u0 vs u1). Whenever there's a genuine income effect on the price-changing good, the compensating amount needed at the poorer reference point differs from the amount needed at the richer one — there's no arithmetic error, just two legitimately different (and both correct) ways of pricing the same welfare change.

steps.heading: Why three different numbers for one price change?
steps.body: Consumer surplus, CV, and EV can all disagree about the exact pound value of the SAME price change because each is built from a different demand curve: CS uses the ordinary (Marshallian) demand curve at the actual income level, while CV and EV each use a Hicksian (compensated) demand curve — but fixed at two DIFFERENT utility levels (u0 for CV, u1 for EV). All three coincide exactly only in one special case: when preferences are QUASILINEAR in the numeraire good (the good whose price ISN'T changing), so there is NO income effect at all on the price-changing good. In that case, Hicksian demand for that good doesn't depend on the utility level chosen, and is identical to Marshallian demand — collapsing CS, CV and EV into a single, unambiguous number.

steps.q: Under quasilinear preferences (no income effect on the price-changing good), what happens to the relationship between CS, CV and EV?
options: They diverge even further from each other than under Cobb-Douglas preferences
They all collapse to exactly the same value, since Hicksian demand for the price-changing good becomes independent of the utility level and matches Marshallian demand
CV becomes undefined
EV always becomes negative
steps.explain: With no income effect on the good whose price is changing, the Hicksian demand curve for that good is the SAME curve regardless of which utility level you fix it at — and it coincides with the Marshallian demand curve too. Since CS, CV and EV are really just three different ways of measuring the area under (variants of) this one demand curve, they all become identical under quasilinearity.

lessons.title: Pareto Efficiency and Social Welfare Functions

steps.heading: Ranking outcomes: economics is about trade-offs
steps.body: It's often said that economics is fundamentally about trade-offs: consumption vs. saving, risk vs. return, inflation vs. unemployment, short-run costs vs. long-run growth. Deciding which trade-offs are actually WORTH making requires some way of ranking different possible outcomes against each other. A social welfare function (SWF) does exactly this: it assigns a single overall 'social welfare' number to any given allocation of utility across individuals in society, reflecting a specific choice about how one person's gain should be weighed against another's loss. But before committing to any particular SWF, there's a much weaker, less controversial way to compare two outcomes — one everyone can agree on.

steps.heading: Pareto improvement: a criterion nobody can object to
steps.body:
An outcome Y is a Pareto improvement over outcome X if Y makes AT LEAST ONE person strictly better off, and makes NO ONE worse off. Formally, if utility for person i is written Ui(·), Y is a Pareto improvement over X if Ui(Y) ≥ Ui(X) for every person i, with strict inequality for at least one person.

The appeal of this criterion is that it requires no controversial value judgement at all: since literally everyone is at least as well off under Y, and someone strictly prefers it, no one could reasonably object to the move. An allocation is called Pareto efficient (or Pareto optimal) if there is NO Pareto improvement available over it — you genuinely cannot make anyone better off without making someone else worse off.

steps.heading: Worked example: checking Pareto comparisons
steps.body:
Consider four possible outcomes, giving (utility to Person 1, utility to Person 2): W=(5,1), X=(1,4), Y=(2,2), Z=(0,0).

Is X a Pareto improvement over Z? Compare term by term: Person 1 gets 1 instead of 0 (strictly better), Person 2 gets 4 instead of 0 (strictly better). NO ONE is worse off, and both are strictly better off — yes, X is a clear Pareto improvement over Z.

Is W a Pareto improvement over Y? Compare: Person 1 gets 5 instead of 2 (better), but Person 2 gets 1 instead of 2 (WORSE). Since someone is worse off, W is NOT a Pareto improvement over Y — and by the same logic, Y is not a Pareto improvement over W either. The Pareto criterion simply CANNOT rank W against Y: from the Pareto perspective alone, they are incomparable.

steps.q: Using outcomes W=(5,1), X=(1,4), Y=(2,2), Z=(0,0), which statement is correct?
options: W is a Pareto improvement over Y, since Person 1's gain is larger than Person 2's loss
The Pareto criterion cannot rank W against Y, since Person 1 gains but Person 2 loses moving from Y to W
Z is a Pareto improvement over every other outcome
All four outcomes are Pareto improvements over each other
steps.explain: Moving from Y=(2,2) to W=(5,1): Person 1 gains (2→5) but Person 2 loses (2→1). Since the Pareto criterion requires NO ONE to be worse off, and here someone is, it cannot declare either outcome a Pareto improvement over the other — they are simply incomparable using this criterion alone.

steps.heading: Pareto efficiency does not mean fair or equal
steps.body: A crucial and often-tested subtlety: Pareto efficiency says NOTHING about how equal or fair an allocation is. An allocation where one person gets everything and another gets nothing can still be perfectly Pareto efficient — if there is truly no way to reallocate that helps the worse-off person without taking something away from the better-off one, the criterion is satisfied, however unequal the outcome looks. This is exactly why economists distinguish EFFICIENCY (are all mutual gains exhausted?) from EQUITY (is the outcome fair?) as two entirely separate questions, and why a policy can be efficiency-improving while still being controversial on fairness grounds, or vice versa.

steps.q: An allocation gives Person 1 everything and Person 2 nothing. Could this allocation still be Pareto efficient?
options: No — Pareto efficiency always requires at least some redistribution toward the worse-off person
Yes — Pareto efficiency only asks whether a further reallocation could help someone without hurting anyone else; it says nothing about fairness or equality of the outcome itself
No — by definition, a Pareto efficient allocation must give everyone equal utility
This is impossible to determine without knowing the specific utility functions
steps.explain: Pareto efficiency is entirely about whether unexploited mutual gains remain — if giving Person 2 anything would necessarily require taking something from Person 1 (making Person 1 worse off), then this maximally unequal allocation IS Pareto efficient, however unfair it may seem on distributional grounds. Efficiency and equity are genuinely separate criteria.

steps.heading: Efficiency of competitive equilibrium, and efficiency without prices
steps.body:
One of the classic results built on this idea (studied more formally in EC202) is that a competitive market equilibrium — where every consumer optimises given prices, every firm optimises given prices, and all markets clear — is typically Pareto efficient, PROVIDED there are no market failures (no externalities, no market power, full information). This is a key part of the intuitive case economists make for markets: not that they produce a FAIR outcome, but that they tend to exhaust all available mutual gains from trade.

Importantly, Pareto efficiency is a property of an ALLOCATION, and doesn't require markets or prices to exist at all in order to be checked — within a household, in a barter economy, or under central planning, you can always ask directly: 'does some other allocation of the same goods make someone better off without harming anyone else?' If the answer is no, the allocation is Pareto efficient, price system or not.

steps.heading: The utilitarian SWF: resolving the cases Pareto cannot rank
steps.body:
A full social welfare function fills the gap the Pareto criterion leaves open. The simplest example is the UTILITARIAN SWF, which simply sums everyone's utility: SWF = ΣᵢUi. Applying this to the earlier example: W has sum 5+1=6, X has sum 1+4=5, Y has sum 2+2=4, Z has sum 0+0=0. This gives a COMPLETE ranking: W > X > Y > Z — in particular, it resolves the W-vs-Y comparison that the Pareto criterion alone could not touch, by declaring W better simply because its total is higher.

But notice the cost of this completeness: the utilitarian SWF implicitly treats one unit of Person 1's utility as worth EXACTLY the same as one unit of Person 2's utility — a specific value judgement that not everyone would accept (an egalitarian SWF, for instance, might instead favour the more equal Y=(2,2) over the more unequal W=(5,1), even though W has the higher sum). This is the fundamental trade-off between the Pareto criterion (judgement-free, but incomplete) and any full SWF (complete, but value-laden).
